# 1.6.0 (November 15th, 2023)

CHANGES

* Upgrade hashicorp/go-msgpack to v2, with go.mod upgraded from v0.5.5 to v2.1.1. [GH-577](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/pull/577)

  go-msgpack v2.1.1 is by default binary compatible with v0.5.5 ("non-builtin" encoding of `time.Time`), but can decode messages produced by v1.1.5 as well ("builtin" encoding of `time.Time`).

  However, if users of this library overrode the version of go-msgpack (especially to v1), this **could break** compatibility if raft nodes are running a mix of versions.

  This compatibility can be configured at runtime in Raft using `NetworkTransportConfig.MsgpackUseNewTimeFormat` -- the default is `false`, which maintains compatibility with `go-msgpack` v0.5.5, but if set to `true`, will be compatible with `go-msgpack` v1.1.5.

IMPROVEMENTS
* Fixed a performance anomaly related to pipelining RPCs that caused large increases in commit latency under high write throughput. Default behavior has changed. For more information see #541.

# 1.4.0 (March 17th, 2023)

FEATURES
* Support log stores with a monotonically increasing index.  Implementing a log store with the `MonotonicLogStore` interface where `IsMonotonic()` returns true will allow Raft to clear all previous logs on user restores of Raft snapshots.

BUG FIXES
* Restoring a snapshot with the raft-wal log store caused a panic due to index gap that is created during snapshot restores.

# 1.3.0 (April 22nd, 2021)

IMPROVEMENTS

* Added metrics for `oldestLogAge` and `lastRestoreDuration` to monitor capacity issues that can cause unrecoverable cluster failure  [[GH-452](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/pull/452)][[GH-454](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/pull/454/files)]
* Made `TrailingLogs`, `SnapshotInterval` and `SnapshotThreshold` reloadable at runtime using a new `ReloadConfig` method. This allows recovery from cases where there are not enough logs retained for followers to catchup after a restart. [[GH-444](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/pull/444)]
* Inclusify the repository by switching to main [[GH-446](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/pull/446)]
* Add option for a buffered `ApplyCh` if `MaxAppendEntries` is enabled [[GH-445](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/pull/445)]

Audit continued; report written to [report.md](/home/nitro/Desktop/consensus-assurance/baseline/runs/2026-10-09_08-06-10-hashicorp_raft-baseline/work/report.md).

Key results this turn:

**Provenance (executed, decisive).** The supplied tree is byte-identical to the upstream released module `github.com/hashicorp/raft@v1.7.3`. A full recursive diff against the module-cache extraction, plus a re-extraction of the module `.zip` itself, produced no differences (only the nested-module dirs `fuzzy/` and `raft-compat/`, which Go excludes from a module zip). The recorded origin hash equals the run brief's `source_identity` (`c0dc6a0b...`, `refs/tags/v1.7.3`). So there is no locally-injected mutation to point at; any real defect would have to be genuinely present in upstream v1.7.3.

**Execution.**
- `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` clean.
- Full `go test ./...` fails only in TCP/loopback tests, which this shell cannot run (its sandbox denies `socket()` outright), plus one flaky test.
- `go test -race` on an in-memory-transport subset: **no data races, no panics**.

**Reproducible observation (not a safety defect).** `TestRaft_HasExistingState` (and, under `-race`, `TestRaft_SnapshotRestore_PeerChange`) intermittently fail ~1-in-6 inside `EnsureSamePeers` with a "peer mismatch." Root cause is a read-lag: `GetConfiguration()` returns the node's *latest* (possibly not-yet-replicated) configuration, and the test asserts convergence within a wall-clock window. Logged in `audit/flaky_hasstate.log`.

**Blocker for remaining coverage.** The ~15 TCP-backed tests (`net_transport`, `tcp_transport`, `integ_test.go`) require the harness's private-loopback exec; nested `bwrap` from this shell fails with `Failed to create NETLINK_ROUTE socket: Operation not permitted`, so I could not clear them here.

No fabricated findings: I have not demonstrated an implementation-level consensus defect, and I explicitly do not claim one. Remaining work (recorded in the report) is to run the TCP suite via the isolated exec, stress the two flaky tests, and scrutinize the pre-vote extension and leader-lease/transfer edge cases — the least-covered paths and the most likely home of a genuine upstream defect.
